vignette:
Liam sits across from me, his large, capable hands resting on his knees. They are the hands of a man who works outdoors-calloused and steady-but they betray a subtle tremor he seems unable to control. At 32, he has the rugged look of the park ranger he is, with a sun-weathered face and clear blue eyes. Those eyes, however, rarely stay still. They scan the room, flicking to the door, the window, and back to me, constantly assessing for threats that don't exist within these four walls.

Two years ago, Liam was on the adventure of a lifetime. A seasoned outdoorsman, he had saved for a solo three-month trek through a remote mountain range in South America. It was the ultimate test of the skills he'd honed his entire career. He describes the first few weeks with a ghost of a smile, recalling the sharp, clean air and the profound silence of the peaks. That was before he stumbled upon a hidden encampment. He was taken swiftly, a burlap sack thrown over his head before he could even process what was happening.

He doesn't-or can't-recount the next ten days in a linear fashion. The story comes out in fragments, disjointed images and sensory details that pierce through the numbness he wraps himself in. He talks about the constant, chilling dampness of the dirt floor he was forced to lie on. He remembers the smell of stale cigarettes and unwashed bodies, the rough texture of the ropes that bound his wrists, and the metallic taste of his own blood. He was interrogated in a language he didn't understand, the questions punctuated by casual, unpredictable violence. The worst part, he says, wasn't the physical pain, but the utter powerlessness. He was an expert in survival, a man who could navigate by the stars and read the forest like a book, yet in that dark, cramped hut, none of his knowledge mattered. He was simply a body, subject to the whims of his captors.

His release was as sudden and inexplicable as his capture. He was drugged, driven for hours, and dumped on the side of a rural road. He eventually made his way to the embassy and back home. His family and friends celebrated his survival, his "incredible story of resilience." But Liam felt he had left the vital parts of himself back in that hut.

Now, the wilderness, once his sanctuary, has become a landscape of triggers. He still works for the Park Service, but he's taken a position at the main visitor center, unable to handle the backcountry patrols he once lived for. The snap of a twig behind him on a trail is no longer a deer; it's the sound of a footstep approaching from behind. The deep shadows cast by the ancient pines at dusk feel suffocating, claustrophobic. He reports having to pull his truck over on the park road, gasping for air, because the isolation he once craved now feels like a prelude to ambush.

His life outside of work has shrunk to the size of his small apartment. He hasn't dated since his return, explaining that he pushed his then-girlfriend away, unable to tolerate the intimacy or explain the chasm that had opened inside him. Sleep offers little respite. He often wakes up thrashing, the phantom feeling of ropes on his wrists, his heart hammering against his ribs. He spends his nights checking the locks on his doors and windows, sitting in the dark, listening. He feels a profound sense of shame, a corrosive belief that he should have been stronger, that he should have seen it coming. The man who once felt at home anywhere in the world now feels safe nowhere at all.
